title: Why are flamingos pink? It starts with dinner

sources.name: Smithsonian’s National Zoo — Flamingo colour and chicks
San Diego Zoo Wildlife Alliance — Flamingo diet and feeding

sections.title: The colour starts in their food
sections.html:
Flamingos are pink because their food contains carotenoids, natural pigments that their bodies process. Those pigments colour the feathers as they grow.

The Smithsonian’s National Zoo explains that flamingos can get them from algae or from brine shrimp that have eaten algae. The colour has travelled through a food chain before arriving at the party.

sections.title: Is it just because they eat shrimp?
sections.html:
Shrimp are part of the story, not the whole answer. Flamingo species eat different mixtures of algae and small aquatic animals. The useful clue is the pigment, rather than one item on the menu.

San Diego Zoo describes their filter feeding: food particles are trapped as water passes through the bill. Different bill structures suit different-sized foods.

sections.title: Are baby flamingos born pink?
sections.html:
No. Chicks hatch with pale white-grey down. Their familiar adult colour develops over time. That fluffy grey bird beside a pink parent has not wandered into the wrong family photograph.

Remember food → pigments → feathers. For another animal surprise, discover why octopuses have three hearts.

description: Flamingos get their pink colour from pigments in their food, not from being born pink. Follow the food chain—and meet the surprisingly grey chicks.
